title: Photo Sharing Launch
summary: A photo app launches publicly at 12,000 rps. 60% of traffic is images, and it's all going through app servers into one SQL database.
scenario: A photo-sharing app leaves beta. Traffic: 12,000 requests per second, 60% of it image and asset downloads.
The current design routes everything through the app servers. Images come from object storage via the app tier, and feed reads and photo uploads all hit a SQL database.
Both the app tier and the database are overloaded. Redesign it for launch: fast, reliable, and under budget.

objectives.label: Average latency at or below 50 ms

hints: Three problems: images shouldn't touch app servers at all, feed reads repeat a lot, and the SQL primary can't absorb the uploads.
Put a CDN in front for static traffic. Add a cache for feed reads. Move photo metadata to a store that scales writes.

Client → CDN, and Client → Load Balancer → Photo API. From the API, connect a Redis Cache (2 × 32 GB), a Message Queue (2 replicas) → NoSQL (2 replicas), and the API → NoSQL directly too. Drop the SQL DB.
explanation: Separate the paths by traffic type. Static bytes go CDN → object storage and never touch your servers. Dynamic reads go cache-first. Writes go async where users don't need to wait.
A CDN is usually the single biggest win for media apps: it absorbs most of the bandwidth at the edge, close to users, and it's cheaper per byte than serving from your own origin.
Uploads in a real system go straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL. The API only records metadata, and a worker generates thumbnails off the queue.
Notice how one change moves the bottleneck: fix images and the DB becomes the bottleneck, fix reads and writes become the bottleneck. Design is about clearing each in order.
